Development of an Intelligent Web System for Analyzing Scientific Articles for Compliance with Scientific Conference Requirements and Generating Recommendations. This report prepares the first probationary-period submission due on 24 October 2026 at 18:00 Asia/Almaty. The project assists authors in checking a manuscript against explicitly supplied conference requirements and produces evidence-linked recommendations.

The current deliverable includes an analysis and design package, an interactive mock prototype and an initial Go intake-validation module. The complete application, external AI integration and empirical benchmark are not implemented. The relevance analysis uses public conference policies and published screening data. A general positive supervisor response was relayed; its exact date, primary evidence and substantive coverage still require verification. Measured system performance remains implementation-stage work.

This revision corrects the checkpoint audit. Research and design artifacts are prepared; the separate user-discussion condition, substantive supervisor evidence and other-participant review remain open. Representative acceptance is recorded separately from those external conditions.

Conference requirements combine document structure, measurable limits and qualitative expectations. Authors must locate these rules, inspect a PDF or DOCX and explain what needs revision. The working problem hypothesis is that a reusable, criterion-level checking workflow can reduce missed requirements and make revision more systematic. Section 2 analyses official policies and published screening data to ground the document-checking requirements; local user demand remains unmeasured.

Primary users are students and early-career researchers preparing conference submissions. A supervisor may inspect the exported results, but the MVP does not require a separate supervisor account or conference-administration role. Initially, validation focuses on English-language, text-based manuscripts and explicit criteria; support for Russian or Kazakh is a later evaluation decision.

The aim is to design and evaluate a locally runnable web system that identifies supported formal and semantic mismatches between a manuscript and user-confirmed requirements, explains findings with source evidence, and recommends concrete revisions. Objectives are to specify requirements; compare related approaches; normalize documents and criteria; implement deterministic and LLM-assisted checks; preserve evidence and run versions; and measure accuracy, coverage, latency and usefulness against declared baselines.

The team justification fixes Vue 3 and Go; detailed parser, storage and model decisions below are engineering proposals pending review.

Scientific submissions face a combination of measurable limits, venue-specific document rules and requirements that need interpretation. This study examines five official conference rule sets, covering six initial-submission profiles, and an independently published conference screening report. Six recent research publications provide a separate basis for choosing an evidence-oriented technical approach.

The strongest operational evidence comes from CHI 2025: organisers report 495 desk rejections among 5,014 complete submissions. Anonymisation, template and length categories account for 229 reported cases. These data establish that submission compliance has observable consequences in at least one real conference process. They do not estimate how many cases our proposed system could prevent. [H]

The policy comparison identifies different page limits and exclusion rules, while the research evidence cautions against treating fluent AI feedback as a verified judgement. Together, these findings support a narrowly scoped assistant: configurable criteria, deterministic checks where possible, evidence-linked interpretation where needed, and explicit uncertainty.

RQ1: Which submission constraints are shared across venues, and which require configurable rules? RQ2: Is there published operational evidence of compliance-related screening? RQ3: What does recent research imply for document processing and AI-generated recommendations?

Sources were selected purposively for relevance to English-language computer-science manuscripts. The policy sample comprises ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2025, ACL 2026, CVPR 2026 and ICLR 2026. ACL long and short papers are separate profiles of one venue, not independent conferences. Policy fields were manually coded from explicit statements; unrecorded information means not coded, rather than no requirement. The comparison concerns initial submissions unless a stage change is explicitly discussed.

Operational counts are transcribed from the official CHI report and recomputed with declared denominators. Research findings are a targeted synthesis, not a pooled experiment or systematic review. The six research sources date from 2023-2025. Official policies cover 2025-2026 events; generic guidance is identified as a current web revision. Sources were accessed on 22 October 2026.

All five sampled rule sets specify a main-text limit, anonymity and a prescribed format or style. Across the six profiles, initial-submission limits take three values: 4, 8 and 9 pages. These are sample descriptions, not estimates of the wider conference population.

The main-text limit cannot be applied to the total PDF page count without identifying excluded sections. The rule configuration also needs a submission stage: ICLR allows 9 pages initially and 10 during discussion/rebuttal and camera-ready preparation. The same guide contains later wording that calls the limit identical while giving 10 pages; a parser must retain the stage-specific context instead of selecting the last number it sees. [G]

Mandatory, recommended and optional are distinct statuses. For example, the NeurIPS checklist is required [B], while ICLR recommends an ethics statement where appropriate [G]. A missing optional statement must not become a generic violation.

A single universal checklist is insufficient for this sample. A profile should retain venue, edition, track, paper type, stage, source location and rule status. Automatically extracted criteria should be editable before a run. This is a design inference from the comparison, not a finding about users' interface preferences.

The ACL event page delegates detailed rules to ARR. Current ARR and ACLPUB guidance can have changed since the event's submission cycle; historical runs require a frozen source version. This analysis records that temporal limitation rather than treating current guidance as an archived January snapshot. [C,E,F]
The official Papers Track report, published in December 2024 for the 2025 conference, records 5,014 complete submissions and 495 desk rejections. It identifies the following categories. [H]

Desk-rejection share: 495 / 5,014 x 100 = 9.87%. The organisers round this to 9.9%. The three categories directly relevant to formal screening in this analysis are anonymization, template and length: 134 + 86 + 9 = 229 cases. Their share is 46.26% of desk rejections and 4.57% of complete submissions.

These categories provide a prioritisation signal for potential checks. They are not a measured detection rate, preventable fraction or forecast of product impact. In particular, template compliance and anonymity can require information beyond extracted plain text. The source also notes missing data in some of its analyses; this calculation uses only the explicitly reported screening table.

The context category is the largest and should not be relabelled as a formatting defect. Scope, scientific completeness and plagiarism likewise require different evidence and judgement. Our MVP should avoid collapsing every screening category into a general AI quality score.

CHI is used as operational evidence, not added to the five-venue policy denominator. Its statistics cannot establish rates for ML/NLP conferences or for our intended student users. Local error prevalence and time savings remain unmeasured.
Reliable feedback is narrower than fluent feedback

Zhou, Chen and Yu (2024) evaluate score prediction and review generation and introduce 197 review-revision multiple-choice questions. Their reported weaknesses include long-paper processing and critical feedback. This motivates evaluating specific failure types rather than assuming a plausible review is correct. The study concerns the models and tasks tested; it does not supply an accuracy estimate for our system. [S02]

Li et al. (2025) analyse 1,683 papers and 6,495 expert reviews using five LLMs. They find stronger descriptive feedback than identification of weaknesses and quality-sensitive criticism. Therefore, our recommendations should be tied to explicit requirements and supporting passages. A conference compliance assistant has a more constrained target than autonomous scientific review. The source is the 2025 arXiv version, whose metadata reports acceptance as an ICDM short paper. [S12]
Evidence and document position need separate evaluation

Buchmann, Liu and Gurevych (2024) introduce LAB, covering six long-document tasks and experiments on five models. Their findings distinguish response quality from attribution quality, particularly for complex claims. A quoted passage should therefore be checked for support, not merely for existence in the document. In our design, citation validation and semantic support are separate checks. [S08]

Liu et al. (2024) show position-sensitive performance in multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, with weaker access to information in the middle of long contexts. This motivates testing relevant evidence at the beginning, middle and end of manuscripts. It does not prove that every current model has the same failure rate or that retrieval will always outperform whole-document input. [S07]
Conversion is an independent source of uncertainty

The Docling Technical Report (Auer et al., 2024) describes document conversion using layout and table-structure models. It offers a candidate conversion approach; its abstract does not establish accuracy on our manuscripts. Parser selection requires local evidence on reading order, headings and tables. [S10]

Nougat (Blecher et al., 2023) investigates optical conversion of academic PDFs into markup, including the semantic difficulty of mathematical content. It supplies an alternative for comparison, not evidence that OCR or formula recovery is already implemented. Low-quality conversion must not silently become a successful compliance result. [S09]

The evidence supports a hybrid design hypothesis: deterministic rules for reliably measurable properties, document-aware evidence selection for interpretive criteria, and abstention when the available representation is inadequate. Whether that design improves accuracy, cost or usefulness must be established by the project's own benchmark.

Official rules contain meaningful variation. Published conference data show real screening cases in categories relevant to compliance checks. Recent research identifies document-conversion, feedback-reliability and evidence-attribution concerns that affect implementation choices.

This study does not measure demand among our target users, their willingness to send manuscripts to an external API, their preferred interface, actual time savings or the accuracy of the proposed system. It does not infer a causal reduction in desk rejection from the CHI counts. No interviews, local usability sessions or manuscript benchmark runs are represented as completed.

The project addresses a documented document-checking problem with a bounded engineering response. Its defensible contribution is an inspectable mapping from confirmed conference rules to manuscript-level findings and revisions. Success should be assessed through correctly detected mismatches, useful evidence and appropriate uncertainty, rather than predicted acceptance or generic review scores.

The assignment separately specifies 3-5 discussions with user representatives or a substantive agreement with the actual client. No completed discussions or client agreement are evidenced. The data analysis remains valid in its narrower scope, but it is not automatically a replacement for that separate condition. PCA-22 tracks actual anonymized discussion records, a substantive client agreement, or explicit approval to accept the analysis instead. No interview findings are claimed.

The review uses 16 sources: 12 research publications or research reports from 2023-2025 and 4 primary technical/product sources. Preprints and technical reports are explicitly labelled. Search terms combined manuscript evaluation, conference compliance, rubric-based evaluation, LLM-as-a-Judge, PDF parsing, attribution, document understanding and retrieval-augmented generation. Primary publication pages, author repositories and official documentation were consulted on 22 October 2026.

Selection favoured work that affects one of four decisions: the reliability of AI feedback, criterion-level evaluation, document conversion, or evidence selection. Vendor pages were used only for documented features. This is a focused engineering review, not a systematic review; it does not claim exhaustive retrieval or a meta-analysis.

Liang et al. [S01] support the potential usefulness of generated manuscript feedback, whereas Zhou et al. [S02] show why helpfulness must not be confused with reliable technical judgment. SEA [S03] offers a staged scientific-review framework; Li et al. [S12] further motivate evaluation of contextual grounding and criticism. For this project, the resulting design choice is to verify bounded criteria and show evidence rather than issue an overall scientific acceptance score.

MT-Bench [S04], G-Eval [S05] and Prometheus [S06] motivate explicit criteria and structured judgments, while exposing transfer and bias concerns. Their tasks are different from conference compliance; their reported performance cannot be reused as our accuracy. Attribute or Abstain [S08] motivates inspectable evidence and abstention. A source anchor must therefore be both structurally valid and semantically supportive; JSON validity alone [D04] cannot demonstrate either correctness or usefulness.

Nougat [S09], Docling [S10] and GROBID [D03] provide different routes to structured scholarly text. The project must measure conversion errors separately, because a missed section in extraction can become a false compliance failure. Lost in the Middle [S07] motivates positional sensitivity tests. Self-RAG [S11] illustrates retrieval-based self-reflection, but retrieval can omit evidence needed for exhaustive checking. A vector database is therefore an option to test, not an assumed requirement.

The project gap is an engineering combination to be validated: author-confirmed conference criteria, explicit formal/semantic check boundaries, traceable PDF/DOCX evidence and reproducible local evaluation. Existing products already cover configurable checks and critique, so universal novelty or superiority is not claimed. The complete source matrix and URLs are provided in the repository.

Four relevant systems are compared across the same eight criteria: Penelope.ai [D01], Paperpal Preflight [D02], SEA [S03] and the Liang et al. scientific-feedback pipeline [S01]. The last two are research systems rather than equivalent commercial products. This distinction is necessary when interpreting reproducibility and feature coverage.

These are source-based comparisons, not hands-on tests. Not established means the reviewed source does not substantiate a capability; it does not prove that capability is absent. The proposed system should be justified by the local user need and evaluated implementation, not by unsupported negative claims about competitors. A promising design emphasis is an author-editable conference rubric with criterion-level provenance and explicit uncertainty.

Four result states avoid conflating absent evidence with compliance: pass, fail, insufficient_evidence and not_applicable. A document with no extractable text must fail the extraction stage rather than receive a compliant result. Criteria that require unsupported visual metadata remain explicitly unverified. Ambiguous requirements must be confirmed by the user before being treated as executable rules.

Evidence contains a block_id and a matching quote; page numbers are nullable and derived from the PDF parser, while DOCX uses stable paragraph/table anchors. The context, use-case and component diagrams describe the same local single-user system. The author operates a Vue client; the Go application coordinates storage, document parsing, rule checks and external LLM requests. The parser and judge are replaceable adapters. The external AI provider is outside the local trust boundary. No separate admin system or multi-user authentication is assumed for the first local MVP.

The backend validates an upload and computes its content hash, stores the file under a generated path, extracts structured blocks, and displays extraction warnings. The user confirms normalized criteria. A versioned analysis run then executes supported rules and semantic checks, validates results and evidence, persists the outcome and returns it for inspection. The Go API owns persistence. It writes original files and extracted blocks to generated local paths, and metadata, immutable criteria versions, runs and findings to relational storage. GET history and GET run read saved data through Go; they do not invoke the LLM again. The component diagram shows direct bidirectional Go/storage connections.

The standalone prototype demonstrates manuscript selection, requirements editing and confirmation, analysis progress, criterion-level results, evidence inspection, filtering and rechecking. A visible demo indicator explains that no PDF parsing or AI request takes place. The demonstration uses a synthetic manuscript so it can be shared without disclosing private research.

The key journey is upload or load a synthetic example, enter criteria, confirm criteria, inspect the mock results and open the evidence for a finding. Empty input, zero-byte files, unsupported file types and files above 20 MiB expose validation messages. Invalid replacement clears the previous selection. Five synthetic findings illustrate all four result states, including not_applicable; all states can be filtered. Inputs are disabled during the mock run and exports retain its filename. Keyboard focus and status announcements are included. The future Vue application will replace the demonstration data with the documented REST contract.

The prototype is a UX artefact and does not establish usability or analysis quality. Usability validation is a later activity: ask target users to complete a task and record time, confusion and comments.

RQ1: does a hybrid rule-plus-LLM pipeline identify supported criterion violations more accurately than rules alone? RQ2: does criterion-level evidence improve the rate of supported explanations compared with one unconstrained whole-document prompt? RQ3: what are the cost, latency and stability trade-offs under fixed files and criteria? These questions remain untested.

Baseline B0 runs deterministic checks only and abstains on semantic criteria. Baseline B1 uses one whole-document LLM prompt with the same available model and documents, a fixed criterion list and no staged evidence validation. Proposed method B2 uses confirmed criteria, deterministic supported checks, section-level evidence and schema/anchor validation. Keep prompts and token limits versioned; compare each method on its eligible criterion types and report common subsets separately.

Plan at least 20 rights-cleared text-based English manuscripts with 8-12 criteria each. Use permitted public papers or author-consented drafts, plus explicitly synthetic controlled variants. Preserve base-document groups so variants never cross development/test boundaries. A proposed split is 8 development and 12 held-out documents. Freeze test labels before tuning prompts. Use two annotators; record initial labels, disagreements and adjudicated labels. Synthetic variants test known violations but cannot substitute for evaluation on real papers.

Create criteria from real, dated conference guidelines, respecting applicable reuse terms. Include missing required sections, abstract-length violations, absent limitations, weakly specified methodology, ambiguous rules, cross-section evidence, unsupported layout requirements and adversarial embedded instructions. Confirm ground-truth semantics with the supervisor or a qualified reviewer. Do not assume the two student annotators alone establish scientific correctness.
